extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, scholars, publishers, composers and artists seeking guidance on copyright and related remedies
extracted.subtask_short: copyright protection for music and prints
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria governing copyright protection, assignment, piracy, and remedies for musical compositions, dramatic works, engravings/prints, maps/charts, and related periodical-publication issues under historic UK statutes and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence sufficient to prove publication of a newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: It was considered sufficient evidence that a person was the publisher of a newspaper, when it was proved that it was sold at his office, and that he, as proprietor of the paper, had given a bond to the stamp-office pursuant to the 29 Geo. III. c. 80 s. 10 for securing the duties on the advertisements, and that he had occasionally applied there respecting the duties on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication of a newspaper may be proved by sale at proprietor's office plus administrative acts (e.g. bond to stamp-office) and by printer testimony that it was published 'in the usual way.' See citations: The King v. Topham; Peake N.P.C. C70; The King v. Pearce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unstamped newspaper admissible in evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Though a publisher is liable to a penalty for not having his newspaper stamped; yet, thus unstamped, it may be given in evidence; for this case is not like that of deeds and agreements, where the acts of parliament expressly declare that no such instrument shall be read in evidence until it is stamped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish statutory bars on unstamped deeds/contracts from evidentiary admissibility of unstamped newspapers in libel or other proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to read extracts to explain or mitigate libel
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain the libel, and to mitigate the damages, the defendant has a right to have read in evidence extracts from a different part of the same newspaper, connected with the subject of the libellous passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants may introduce contextual extracts from the same publication to explain or reduce liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chancery discovery for anonymous proprietors of libellous paper
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person has been libelled in a newspaper, and suspects the author to be a proprietor not named in the affidavit, he may file a bill in Chancery for a discovery of the names of any persons concerned in it; the defendants are not allowed to plead or demur, but must make the discovery required; such information, when obtained, cannot be used in any other proceeding, except in that for which the discovery is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chancery compulsory discovery is available to identify unnamed proprietors in libel cases, but the discovery is limited to the purpose of the bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether a musical composition is protected by the copyright acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical compositions are books to be protected by the statute of 8 Anne, and those acts of parliament which have enlarged the benefits to be derived from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music (including single sheets) falls within 'books and other writings'—courts have held music may be written and protected as a book (see Bach v. Longman; Lord Mansfield's reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of protection for musical compositions (whole or part)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not material whether the matter pirated be a whole book of music, or some one tune of a particular name in a work bearing a different title; a musical composition published on a single sheet is protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection extends to complete works and to individual tunes extracted from larger works; a single sheet is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property in music equals property in a book; vests in the composer
rubrics_metrics.description: The property in a piece of music is exactly the same as that in a book. The statute vests the property in the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private regulations (e.g., theatre claiming all songs belong to establishment) cannot derogate from statutory rights of the composer (see Lord Kenyon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of musical copyright must be in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment of the copyright of music must be in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even long acquiescence and a receipt for price did not transfer the copyright absent a written assignment (cases cited: Power v. Walker; Morris v. Kelly). Equity may decline injunctions until common-law right is established where author has permitted wide copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piracy by taking down music at the theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who can write music as they hear it publicly rehearsed may be prevented by injunction from violating the property of the composer by publishing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have enjoined publication based on shorthand or musical transcription taken from public performances (see note: piracy by taking down at Theatre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed dramatic compositions are books within statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays or dramatic pieces of every description, when printed and published, are books within the meaning of the statute of 8 Anne, c. 19; and no one with impunity can multiply copies of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printing and publishing a play invokes statutory copyright protections analogous to books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of unpublished/manuscript dramatic compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The protection of the law is also extended to a dramatic composition whilst it is yet in manuscript, and has not been publicly represented, in the same manner as to manuscripts in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunctions are granted to restrain persons from acting and also from printing plays which have not been published; equity protects unpublished dramatic works (see Macklin v. Richardson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting a play is not necessarily 'publication' at common law
rubrics_metrics.description: In the common law courts it has been decided that proof that the defendant acted a piece on the stage of which the plaintiff had bought the copyright was not evidence of a publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance alone may not support an action at common law for copyright infringement, although equity may grant injunctions to stop performance (Coleman v. Walthen; Murray v. Elliston).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity remedies for performance of printed dramatic works
rubrics_metrics.description: In equity injunctions have been and continue to be granted, to stop the performance of printed dramatic pieces at the instance or request of the author or proprietors of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where common law remedies are limited, equity can enjoin performances to protect proprietors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory protection for engravings/prints and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A property in prints is secured to the inventors and engravers by statutes (e.g., 8 Geo. II. c. 13, 7 Geo. III. c. 38, 17 Geo. III. c. 57); provisions cover historical prints, portraits, conversations, landscapes, architecture, maps, charts, plans, and 'any other prints whatsoever.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engravings/prints (including maps/charts) are protected similarly to books; early acts granted 14 years, later extended to 28 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to engrave day of publication and proprietor's name on plate/print
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 8 Geo. II. act the day of publication, and the name of the proprietor, must be truly engraved on each plate and print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is judicial disagreement whether this is a mandatory condition to vest the right or only directory; some judges (Hardwicke, Ellenborough) treated it as directory while others (Kenyon, Buller) regarded insertion as essential to enforcement. Consider the public importance of the date and proprietor's name for monopoly notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prints accompanying letterpress are fully protected
rubrics_metrics.description: The prints that ornament and illustrate works are as fully protected by these statutes as those which are published alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative plates are not merely accessory; an artist making bona fide drawings from text may acquire copyright in resulting engraving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter of an engraving is not monopolizable; only particular work protected
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjects of engravings are almost always general ones, and cannot be monopolized. Each particular print is protected by the statutes: but the subject is open to every artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may take engravings from the same picture or subject; the jury decides whether a later work is a servile imitation (piracy) or an independent drawing from the same subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: No copyright in immoral/obscene/libellous prints
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be any property in an immoral, obscene, or libellous book. That doctrine equally applies to pictures and prints; an action of assumpsit cannot be maintained for the value of them, even against a purchaser at the suit of the person who sold them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illicit content is non-protectable and cannot underpin a copyright claim or recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property in prints vested in inventor/engraver, not mere commissioner
rubrics_metrics.description: The property in prints is vested in him who shall invent and design, engrave, &c., or from his own works and inventions shall cause to be designed and engraved any print; but a person procuring a drawing to be made was held not entitled to a monopoly derived from the statutes if he did not assist in its design or formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creator/engraver holds statutory right; mere commissioning without creative contribution may not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment/purchase of a plate permits printing by purchaser
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who shall thereafter purchase any plate for printing from the original proprietors thereof may print and reprint from the same, without incurring the penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchase of the physical plate transfers the practical ability to print; assignment and transfers are recognized—assignee may maintain actions for piracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent to copy must be in writing with two witnesses (statutory form)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary, before a print can be copied with impunity, to obtain 'the consent of the proprietor thereof in writing, signed by him in the presence of two witnesses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory formalities for consent/assignment are required under the acts; follow written-witnessed form where prescribed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of piracy for prints and engravings
rubrics_metrics.description: A piracy is committed, if any person 'in any manner copy in the whole or in part by varying, adding to, or diminishing from the main design' of any print whatsoever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facsimile reproduction is a gross infringement; 'varying' or small alterations may still constitute piracy if they amount to a servile imitation of the main design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seller/importer liability for pirated prints (knowledge not required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one who sells or imports for sale any pirated copies of an engraving is liable to the penalties inflicted by the statutes. The vendor of a print which, with some trifling variations, is a copy of the main design of another print is liable to an action for damages although he did not know that the print which he was selling was a piracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes have been interpreted to impose strict liability on vendors/importers for distributing pirated prints; lack of knowledge is not a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for infringement: injunctions, actions for damages, accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: By the statutes and equity practice the remedies for piracy include injunctions to restrain printing or acting, actions for damages, and an account of profits; later statutes (e.g., 17 Geo. III. c. 57) provided special actions and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity often supplements common-law limitations by granting preventive relief (injunctions) and accounting remedies; consult the particular statutory provisions for costs and procedural forms.
